relations.subject: index:group-aggregate-pushdown
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - family membership; the mechanism is described exactly as the family is (the Query engine asks the Indexer to do work it would otherwise do itself)
relations.evidence: Without grouping and aggregate pushdown, if a query contained aggregation and/or grouping, the query engine would fetch all relevant data from the indexer and group the data itself, even if the query was covered by an index. With grouping and aggregate pushdown, the query intelligently requests the indexer to perform grouping and aggregation in addition to range scan. The Indexer has been enhanced to perform grouping, COUNT(), SUM(), MIN(), MAX(), AVG(), and related operations.

relations.subject: index-type:array-index
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - two conjoined conditions on the array case: the array key must use DISTINCT rather than ALL, and the SATISFIES clause must be an equality
relations.evidence: In this case, the predicates are on the leading keys up to and including the array key. Therefore, indexer can efficiently do the grouping as seen by the optimal plan below. It's important to note the array index key is created with a `DISTINCT` modifier (not the `ALL` modifier) to get this optimization and that the `SATISFIES` clause in the `ANY` predicate must be that of equality (that is, `v = "%a%"`).

notable_absence.finding: The page's Table 1 (Aggregate Comparison) is presented as the authoritative support matrix - four index-field cases crossed with four aggregate groups - and it contradicts the page's own worked examples. The row 'Supports SUM() and COUNT()' is marked '-' (unsupported) in the column 'Aggregate on Non-Array Index Field', while Example B on the same page pushes 'SELECT geo.alt, geo.lat, SUM(geo.lon), AVG(id), COUNT(DISTINCT geo.lon) FROM airport ... GROUP BY geo.alt, geo.lat' against a plain composite index on (geo.alt, geo.lat, geo.lon, id) - all non-array fields - and says 'The query plan shows that the index scan handles grouping and aggregation'. Example C, Example 13 (COUNT of a string field) and the appendix's own SUM example (Table 3, 'EXPLAIN Text in Example 15 (Aggregate)', aggregate: SUM) do the same. So either the table is wrong or thirteen examples are, and a reader has no way to tell which. I have therefore extracted the prose rule ('the only aggregate functions that are supported are SUM(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX(), and AVG()') and NOT extracted Table 1 as an enum or as a set of doesNotSupport relations, because doing so would put a false negative into the ontology with a quotable citation behind it - exactly the failure mode the evidence gate exists to prevent, dressed as compliance. This is the single most consequential defect I found in the batch and it wants a docs issue. Second, smaller absence: Table 1's ARRAY_AGG() row is '-' in all four columns, which agrees with the Limitations list, so the table is not uniformly stale - only that one row.

cross_component_finding: This page is the origin of the storage-engine/storage-mode collision the registry already records, and it does not resolve it: 'Grouping and aggregate pushdown is supported on both storage engines: Standard GSI and Memory Optimized GSI (MOI).' Standard GSI and MOI are the two user-selectable storage MODES (promoted as index:standard-storage and index:memory-optimized-storage); the actual engines a level down - Plasma for standard, Nitro for memory-optimized, Forestdb historically - are named on storage-modes.md and appear NOWHERE in any of the five pages in this batch. So no storage-engine:* id is evidenceable from this batch at all, and this page actively supplies contrary usage. My reading is that the docs use 'engine' loosely wherever the distinction does not matter to the reader, and precisely only on the page that has to explain the difference. Phase 2 should not treat this sentence as evidence about engines in either direction; it is evidence that the term 'storage engine' is overloaded in the Capella docs, which is what the existing collision note on index:standard-storage says. I minted the predicate isSupportedOnStorageMode rather than bend a promoted one, and deliberately named it for the MODE level so the relation cannot be misread as an engine claim later.
cross_product_finding: Title and abstract disagree about what this page is: the H1 is 'Grouping and Aggregate Pushdowns' but the abstract underneath it reads 'SQL++ Pushdowns optimize the performance of SQL++ queries by supporting grouping and aggregate expressions' - i.e. the abstract names the whole pushdown family and then describes one member of it. index_pushdowns.md is the page that actually owns 'SQL++ Pushdowns' as a subject, and its abstract is the family definition ('Index Pushdowns are performance optimizations where the Query engine pushes more of the work down to the Indexer'). Two pages therefore claim the family in their abstracts, which is presumably why the corpus ended up with the family at recurrence 1-3 and no page recognised as defining it. On the version question: every dated claim here has been stripped for Capella and left ungrounded - 'The Indexer has been enhanced to perform grouping...', 'Currently, the only aggregate functions that are supported are...', 'The following are currently not supported' - and the image filenames still carry the Server release that introduced the feature (GBAP_Ex0_QP_before55.png, GBAP_Ex0_QP_after55.png, GBAP_55execution-*.svg, GBAP_pre55execution-*.svg, i.e. 5.5). The version survives only in asset names, which is not extractable evidence and is not a fact about Capella either; I have recorded no availableSince relation from this page.
